title: Composition analysis (SCA) and vulnerabilities in dependencies

videos.script: linkbox's two requirements files name nine packages. Install them, and you get thirteen. {{tree}} Most of the code it runs was written by somebody else. When a flaw turns up in that code, it is published as an advisory, often under three names at once. {{names}} Today you audit linkbox's pins with pip-audit. It prints twenty-nine rows. They come down to fifteen flaws, in four packages. {{audit}} Then you read them. Most need something linkbox does not do. A session it never uses. A Windows server it does not run on. {{reading}} You will meet three numbers that sound alike and are not. CVSS says how bad. EPSS says how likely. KEV says it has already happened. {{scores}} A second tool reads the same files and disagrees, and you will find out why. Then comes the smallest move that clears the list, a test run that proves nothing broke, and a stage that keeps the list clear. Its first run fails, on a test tool that never ships. You will see why it still counts. {{pipeline}}
